utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-99-37-PT and case number IT-01-50-I, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll hear the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court. Dirk Ryneveld, Senior Trial Attorney for the Kosovo indictment, along with Madam Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte and my colleague Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff for the Croatia indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Stephen Kay, Queen's Counsel of the bar of England and Wales.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Michail Wladimiroff, member of the bar of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branislav Tapuskovic, member of the bar from Belgrade and an attorney from Belgrade, a member of the bar of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The purpose of this hearing is to deal with four matters which we will deal with in this order: First of all, the hearing of argument on a number of motions; secondly, the reading of the Kosovo indictment and the accused to enter a plea on one count if necessary; the Initial Appearance on the Croatia indictment; and finally a Status Conference. As to time, we have available today and, if necessary, tomorrow morning. However, the reading of the indictments is going to take some time, but nonetheless I hope it may be possible to finish today. We begin with the motions hearing, and the matters to be considered are these: First of all, a Prosecution motion for leave to file a second amended indictment, and then various preliminary motions and documents from the accused together with a brief on jurisdiction from the amicus curiae. We'll deal with these motions in this way: that first we will hear the arguments of the Prosecution and the amicus on the motion to amend the indictment; we will next hear the arguments of the amicus and then the Prosecution on the preliminary motions; and finally we will hear the accused on all motions. We begin then with the Prosecution motion for leave to file a second amended indictment, this is under Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which provides that the Prosecutor may amend an indictment after the assignment of a case to a Trial Chamber with the leave of the Chamber, after having heard the parties. It may be of assistance if I summarise the issues which are raised under this motion. The motion states that the reasons for the amendment are as follows: First, to reflect the link between killings in Kosovo and the bodies found in mass graves near Belgrade; second, to add an additional count of forcible transfer - this relates to the Kosovo Albanians who were internally displaced within Kosovo rather than actually deported; thirdly, to break down the allegation of persecution in Count 4 - this amendment seeks to particularise the various persecutions and to replace the earlier very general allegation. Fourth, to add a new section on individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. This is said to be an order to specify what the motion calls "common purpose liability." As the Chamber understands it, the amendment seeks to clarify the Prosecution case in this respect and spell out that the Prosecution rely on a joint criminal enterprise in which each of the accused participated. Fifthly, to add three new sites from which the deportations took place and to expand on others, adding more background, and this includes a number of allegations of sexual assault and destruction which were carried out during the deportation operations. There are also various stylistic changes and the rearrangement of some parts of the material. Now, that's intended to be a brief summary of the scope of the amendments, which on the whole, speak for themselves. Now, I'm going to turn to the amicus first. Mr. Wladimiroff, we got your letter of last Friday stating that you wouldn't file a brief on this motion, but there might be some procedural issues to be raised. Is there anything you want to raise on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no further observations at this stage, Your Honour, but maybe later on we may come back to the procedural aspects of any amendment if given leave by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We could hear you better if you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We heard that. So you don't want to make any points about the amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But there may be some subsequent issues which arise out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can deal with them in the Status Conference --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- when we will be timetabling the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's what we had in mind, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will hear any submissions from the accused on this issue in due course. We go on to deal next with the preliminary motions, and in this connection, we have the following motions and other documents, all of which we've read: A motion from the accused of the 9th of August of which he's asked us to consider paragraph 8 only, which we've done; a response from the Prosecution filed on the 16th of August; a presentation, as it was termed, filed by the accused on the 30th of August, relating mainly to the alleged illegality of the Tribunal. This we will treat also as a motion. The brief of the amicus curiae on jurisdiction filed on the 19th of October. This adopts and expands the arguments of the accused. And finally, the response from the Prosecution of the 26th of October. As to the argument, we'll hear the amicus first, then the Prosecutor, and finally, the accused. Who wants to start for the amicus?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Each of us will deal with matters raised in the brief. We have not much to say in addition to what we already wrote in our brief. We have some observations to make, and I will start to do so. First of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say, just to make it clear, that we've had those submissions, for which we are grateful. We have had the chance to read them, so there is no reason to repeat either what you've said or indeed what the Prosecutor has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's exactly what we had in mind, Your Honour. We are not here to repeat things that have already been written or said. The first observation I want to make deals with the position of the amicus curiae and the position of the accused. We pointed out in our brief that the accused should have full opportunity to express himself and to make any statement that is relevant to argue his case. Here, perhaps it would make sense -- perhaps I'll stop here, because while I'm talking, all things happen here, and I have no clue what's going on. Perhaps I should move a little bit to the right. There's little room here too, Your Honour, but we'll try to do it. First of all, I want to say that the amicus curiae, during the pre-trial position, each of us, we feel that we should not raise issues that have not been raised by the accused. So at this stage, we feel appropriate to react to issues that have been raised by the accused. That's for the very reason that we do not want to replace him in terms of raising issues. It's for the accused to raise the issue and we are there to comment on that by assisting the Court in supplying legal reasoning for the argument raised by the accused. So in this approach we feel that the Court should allow the accused the broadest possible room to manoeuvre to argue his case, and as we have said in our brief, that also may include reasons which, on the face of it, might not directly be legal reasons but, more or less, political reasons, because the establishment of the Tribunal, his main challenge, also includes, as we have set out, possible political reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I have heard your explanation as to the understanding of your role. I understand what you have said, but in my view, it is perfectly open to the amici to raise any arguments that they wish so long as it will assist the Chamber, and that is perfectly clear from the motion, from the ruling that the Chamber gave. So I understand what you have done, but for the purposes of the rest of the trial, I think it is important that you understand that your role is a bit wider than that. It is not simply to react to arguments raised by the accused. You are there to assist the Chamber in the consideration of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We understand that, Your Honour. What I tried to explain is at this stage, during pre-trial, having the first motion, we feel that we should approach the matter in a very delicate and diplomatic way, find our way through this method of not being overreactive to anything that's going on or taking initiative where we have no idea what the consequences are. So we start in a very moderate way and develop from there. And that's the reason why we do not feel it appropriate to raise issues at this stage, at the very beginning, that have not been raised by the accused. We may do so later, but not at this stage, because we feel it's for the accused to guide all of us, what he is looking for, what kind of arguments he's looking for, to tell the Court what he is thinking, what he wants. It's not for us to narrow that possibility. So we are very, very, let's say, moderate at the very beginning, and we will develop from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I understand the conservative approach that you have taken, but please understand that your role is a bit wider than that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We may come to that, Your Honour. I am confident that at the end of the day, and that's more than today, I hope that the amici curiae will be able to do what we have to do in the interest of the accused and to assist the Court in finding the right answers to issues that have been raised in this Court. But please allow us to start as delicately as we can. Perhaps I should move on to the next issue I want to touch on. It's a very brief observation as well, because actually we feel everything has been said in our brief. That's the issue of whether previous decisions of the Court or the Appeals Chambers are binding or not. The amici curiae are perfectly aware of the decision in the Aleksovski case, and we are also perfectly aware of what the Appeals Chamber has said there. However, we also believe that whereas in the Statute there is no guidance on the matter that we are now discussing, it is not expressed by the Statute, nor by the Rules, how to deal with the matter. It is, by itself, a matter of case law, how to understand the issue. The Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case found that generally, in common law jurisdiction, there is more binding with previous decisions than in civil law jurisdictions because there is no doctrine there. I think there is some logic in that observation, because if law or a system derives from a statutory system where most issues have been described in the Statute, there's less reason to rely on previous decisions of courts interpreting those statutes; while in common law, people take more precedents from previous decisions and therefore the system of previous decisions, the case law, is more important for the functioning of the system itself. Different from the Appeals Chamber, we feel that in the system of the Tribunal, there is a Statute, there are Rules. One may argue that those Rules may not be complete in terms of dealing with all possible issues, but as a matter of fact, they are dealing with all possible issues on a basis that may be different from what one would see in the Statute, for example, on the European continent. But still there are Rules. The answers are in the Rules and in the Statute. From that point of view, we argue that there is no need to rely on previous decisions in the meaning that they are absolute -- they are absolutely binding. We feel that previous decisions have the importance of being authoritative and they should be of guidance for the Judges, and they should follow them unless they may depart from them, so to say, unless there are cogent reasons in the interests of justice not to do so. So it is not an absolute thing, it is a relative thing. Now, as we have said in our brief, we believe that, on the merits of the case at hand, the Trial Chamber is free to depart from previous decisions and to see whether there are any specific circumstances or arguments raised by the accused or enlightened by the amicus curiae, and therefore the Tadic appeals decision is of very authoritative importance to this Trial Chamber but on the basis of guidance. Now, if you carefully study what we have said, and you have done so, you will realise that we are not actually challenging the Tadic decision. We are following it, and we argue that on the basis of that decision - we'll come to that later - we advise the Trial Chamber to ask for an advisory opinion of the ICJ. We are not saying that the Trial Chamber should rule differently to the Tadic appeals decision. And actually, in the Tadic appeals decision, the issue has not been raised, so it's a novelty. Let me see if there is any other reason to make more observations about this one. The next issue will be discussed by Mr. Kay, and that is the issue Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of independence of the OTP or perhaps the Tribunal. So I will give him the floor, if you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Could the Registrar come, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm dealing with two matters in relation to the brief of the amici curiae filed on the 19th of October. The first of those matters is set out at paragraph 10 of our brief and takes in paragraph 11, and then I'll go on to deal with paragraphs 12 and 13, which is the right of this Tribunal to try a head of state and so is, therefore, an argument raised by the accused concerning the right of state sovereignty. Dealing with the first matter, it's quite clear from the points raised by the accused in his correspondence and various documents that he has asserted that this Tribunal is incapable of giving a fair trial because of its failure in relation to impartiality. One of the key fundamental principles for any valid court of law is the principle of impartiality. Without there -- that, there can be no rule of law and no right to a fair trial. I appreciate this point has been taken several times before in the history of the Tribunal, but that doesn't preclude him in being able to raise the matter. In many respects, this argument of impartiality can be linked up with the issue at the end of the brief filed which the amici curiae, which really concerns the right of these judges, so to speak, to judge themselves in relation to their validity. Mr. Wladimiroff will be addressing you at the end of our submissions on that last feature of the brief of the amici, which starts at paragraph 19 and relates to the test of independence and the proposition that for this court to be validated, it should be validated by a principle organ of the UN, being the International Court of Justice. I won't deal with that argument now as he will, but the point I make is that this issue of impartiality is very much bound up within the validation of the Tribunal. The accused has stated, within the various documents, that the pressure on this Tribunal from external sources to try him and others makes the whole culture of the Tribunal unfair and biased against him, and that's notwithstanding any issue that there may be concerning the right to try him in the first place. The indictment that was issued against him in 1999, at the time of conflict, was as the result of the Security Council urging the Prosecutor to take action in relation to events in Kosovo. Before that time, it appears from the court records there was no public or secret indictment against him. It wasn't until those political events in 1999 that the first indictment was issued as against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The document on which you rely, I think was from the Security Council in March 1998, according to my note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 31st of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The indictment didn't come until a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Obviously there's preparation of these matters. And when that indictment came out, the accused, at that time, was in the middle of a situation of international conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was merely urging the Prosecutor to investigate violations of international humanitarian law. Are you saying that the Security Council shouldn't have done that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a pressure upon the Prosecutor, whose job is derived from the Security Council in the first place, that it would be difficult to say that that party could, thereafter, act independently, and that's the point that's being made here in the submissions of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, in order to substantiate that, wouldn't you have to go a little further and show that that pressure was applied to the Prosecutor in her decision to indict Mr. Milosevic? Is there any evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With respect, I think it's for the Prosecutor to prove there wasn't. It's impossible for an accused or a party in any other position to prove a negative. We're simply not in possession of any of the facts or any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you are making the allegation of a breach of independence. In my view, the onus is on you. You are alleging the lack of impartiality on the part of the Prosecutor. The onus is on you to show that lack of impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What's being asserted here is that there is a suspicion, a reasonable supposition that that could have been the position. As far as the accused is saying within his documents, it would be the definite nature of the allegation. If an assertion such as that is being made in relation to jurisdiction, surely it's for the party who is seeking to establish the jurisdiction to prove to the contrary. For an accused or any other person to take such an argument on the basis of evidence that is not in his possession and would probably never be in his possession in terms of documents or material evidence, it really amounts to an impossibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got to make some sort of showing that there is an absence of impartiality or independence as a result of an urging by the Security Council, not to prosecute this case but to investigate, as I say, violations of international humanitarian law. It may be you can't take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Perhaps this is the sort of issue that when an indictment is confirmed, in view of the general circumstances in which the indictment arose, that the Prosecution should seek to justify the position of the issuance of the indictment in the first place, and it may well be that in the early procedural stages that that is when such a course should have been taken on enquiry by the Court itself, the Confirming Judge, Judge Hunt, in relation to the reasons for the issue of the indictment. We have cited an example within our brief that arose in relation to the manner of detention of the accused, which can be looked at as being an example, if you like, of the kind of impartiality that he asserts. He has been forbidden from speaking to the media or the press, whereas other organs of the Tribunal are in a position to be able to do so. From his perspective, that can be seen as an impartial regulation of the respective positions of the parties. But this issue of impartiality is fundamental to his right to a fair trial, and in many respects, that's why we say the proposition at the end of our brief is the proposition that is the true test of validity. Shall I turn now to the second argument that I'm dealing with? Unless Your Honours have any further issues, outside of that which we've written in our text concerning the issue of impartiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If you'd like to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This relates to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal against him as an individual, as the former President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Court knows and the Prosecution has cited, as indeed we cited the Article 7, subarticle (2) of the Statute that states those acting in their official capacity as head of state may be subject to the jurisdiction or be held criminally responsible for acts before this Tribunal. However, this is an issue here that is probably the oldest and most fundamental rule of the governance between states, and that is the principle of state sovereignty. History is full of examples of attempts to prosecute former heads of state, as we have cited in our brief, none of which were put into effect, and the position of President Milosevic here, one can say properly, is now unique if not historic. The Prosecution, in their response, have cited the case of Prime Minister Kambanda in relation to the Rwanda Tribunal, but that was a plea of guilty and that was not an issue that had to be decided by the Court itself upon this issue of state sovereignty. As I said, the oldest and most fundamental principle that has, by international customary law, governed the relationships between states, which has in fact been inviolable, has been the issue that a state retains its sovereignty and its leader cannot be put on trial for acts committed in that official capacity of acting on behalf of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you must be aware of the vast number of instruments which contain a provision similar to Article 7(2), and I believe you should be aware that by this time, the provision in Article 7(2) reflects a rule of customary international law. With the development of the doctrine of individual criminal responsibility, which commenced after the Second World War, a number of instruments incorporated and reflected that principle; Article 7 of the Nuremberg Charter, Article 6 of the Tokyo Tribunal Charter; Article 4 of the Convention for the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide; and most recently Article 27 of the Rome Statute for the International Criminal Court. At this time, I'm at a loss as to how you could argue that the principle in Article 7(2) is anything but a rule of customary international law in relation to the kind of crimes with which the accused is charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Article 7(2), of course, arises from a Statute that arose from the Security Council, and as one looks at the materials and documents filed by the accused, his principal argument is that this was not a tribunal that was set up by the General Assembly of the United Nations but by the Security Council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the question of whether what is in Article 7(2) reflects the rule of international customary law. The fact that it came from the Security Council doesn't go to that question. What determines whether it is a rule of customary law is primarily two things: state practice, how wide-spread the state practice is, and principally the feeling among states that there is a legal obligation to abide by that rule, the opinio juris. And all of the instruments I have cited, including most recently the Rome Statute, clearly reflect this. So I can't understand the argument coming at this stage. Perhaps immediately after the Second World War, but not some 50 years after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, no previous heads of state have been subject to a trial, and that is a point in itself probably worth making on this issue. The international customary law in relation to state sovereignty still retains itself as a principle. I take Your Honour's point that in relation to these particular violations, that there have been a number of moves within the international community for the trial of violations of humanitarian law, and that has to be recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, let us take the recent case from your own jurisdiction, the Pinochet case, where the House of Lords held that Senator Pinochet was not entitled to immunity in respect to acts of torture and conspiracy to commit torture alleged to have been committed in his capacity as a head of state. I would draw your attention particularly to what Lord Millett said that: "In future, those who commit atrocities against civilian populations must expect to be called to account if fundamental human rights are to be properly protected. In this context, the exalted rank of the accused can afford no defence." Another example of the state practice contributing to the customary character of the rule reflected in Article 7 of the Tribunal's Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the interesting thing was, of course, Senator Pinochet was returned to his own country and wasn't, in fact, extradited to Spain in the event, and we in our brief cite the examples of Pinochet and Noriega.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was extradited or returned on grounds which have nothing to do with the validity of the principle that we are examining now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And a national decision doesn't bind an international court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't bind it, but it goes to the question of the development of custom, of a customary rule of law. It is quite clear that decisions of national courts can be considered in determining whether a rule of customary law has developed. That's very evident, and no citation is needed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And far be it for me in any way to diminish the standing of my own House of Lords. But as far as that decision was concerned, which also involved at one stage an issue of impartiality, which I have held myself back from, mentions earlier on, that decision by that national jurisdiction which they said reflected international customary law, we say, at the end of this brief, is an issue that another organ should decide for this Court, an organ of long-standing international stature, which is a United Nations organ with great experience in dealing with international affairs and the affairs of the United Nations, which is the International Court of Justice. The self-validation process that has been evident within this Tribunal has led to the apparent feeling of impartiality by those over whose affairs it seeks to regulate. I just say that because of the time-honored maxim: Justice must not only be seen to be done, it must be done as well. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your colleague is going to argue that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't preempt him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Far be it for me either. But the point here that this issue of state sovereignty that the accused has raised on his own behalf is a valid and historic argument that, if one looks at the history rather than the political intent, has shown to be a rule that has been applied in many circumstances. And that is what he is pleading on his behalf as a valid reflection of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I think you've covered the points, unless there's anything else you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, add to what Mr. Kay said. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Let's accept that Article 7(2) reflects international law if one accepts that national developments altogether is an expression of a growing understanding between nations and peoples, that such a custom is the right expression of the law. But the real issue then is if Article 7(2) is supposed to reflect international -- to reflect a customary international law, does the wording of Article 7(2) reflect international law? Now, there we have a problem. According to Article 7(2), if we deal with functional responsibility, the test is, to say it very simply, knowledge or awareness, power, and negligence or failure to correct. That may be right for commanders, because there is enough evidence to argue that that test is valid under international -- under customary international law, to see whether a commander is assuming responsibility for what he did in that capacity; but we wonder if such evidence is available if it comes to a head of state. When we argue here, is the test as provided in Article 7(2) the right test to apply to a head of state? So if the Court will agree with that, there is more to the test than what is in Article 7(2). In that respect, Article 7(2) does not reflect customary international law. Now, before moving on, let me reflect for a moment again on the position of the amicus curiae. The Court has put it to Mr. Kay that if you raise an issue, there should be a good showing. In general, we would accept that, but we are not the Defence lawyers of Mr. Milosevic; we are amicus curiae. And as I tried to explain at the very beginning, at this stage, at this very stage, at the very beginning where we have been recently appointed, we react to objections, observations made by the accused. Now, we tried to explain to the Court what the accused is saying. So if there is a showing, the showing should be by the accused and not on the amicus curiae. What I'm saying here is the onus of a showing of the amicus curiae may not necessarily be the same as the onus on the accused. We are not one unit. It's not one thing, the defence, Mr. Milosevic, and the amicus. So if we argue -- actually, perhaps it's not argue. If we translate what the accused says and we argue on the basis of that translation what the meaning is, what perhaps the consequences might be for your court and we advise the Court how to see it, to take into account other arguments related to what the accused has said, it is a little bit difficult to find out at this stage what exactly is the onus on us. Perhaps we will find the right answers later on. At this stage, we believe it's not quite clear if there is a full onus on us. That's a matter to be studied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it was a figure of speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- not a precise onus. We are all finding our way with the position of amicus --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and the role.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, let me move on to the issue I was going to cover. That is the advisory opinion. We have written in our brief that if one studies the literature on the Appeals Chamber's decision in the Tadic case, one of the comments that has been made is the issue of should a court consider its own jurisdiction, its own competence? I'm fully aware that the issue is a common issue in most jurisdictions. At the end of a column, one judge at the end of it, for example, Supreme Court, should judge its own competition -- competence. Here we have a different situation. We are discussing not the competence on the usual issues, but we are discussing the competence in terms of the establishment, the legality of the establishment. That is not a thing that usually is debated in the national setting at the end of the column by, for example, a Supreme Court. So I think some authors are right if they say it could perhaps have been done better if someone else was to refute that. So departing from that point, we believe that it is possible for your Trial Chamber not to refer the case, as the Prosecution asserts, but to consider the possibility of asking an advisory opinion and ruling yourselves on the basis of that advisory opinion. It's your possibility to rule on the matter, but we advise to split up in refining yourself to the formal function of taking the decision but for the substance asking an advisory opinion. Now, under the Charter and under the Statute of the ICG -- the ICJ as well, it is not impossible to do, either by asking it yourself if you believe you've got an inherent authority to do so, or by asking the General Assembly or the Security Council to allow you to do so. And the amicus curiae have found no precedent, no argument why you should not be allowed to ask of such leave. And actually, talking about showing, the Prosecution has not shown there is any valid legal argument that would bar such a request. And we have not seen or heard any argument which explains why the General Assembly or why the Security Council would deny such a question. So we believe it is a possibility which should be pursued, and we believe the Trial Chamber seriously consider that avenue to see whether the answers or the opinion of the ICJ would confirm or attribute or perhaps not confirm the Tadic decision of the Appeals Chamber but is heading for a totally different direction. And then at the end of the day, I think there won't be any criticism any more, because then indeed, a set of judges who are not in force have advised this Court how to proceed. So we believe there's not reason to simply deny it. I think it's a serious consideration to avoid any further criticism on the issue of being independent or being impartial. That's our submission on this issue. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, we'll consider that. Yes, are there any more submissions? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not dwell on matters which my learned colleagues Mr. Kay and Mr. Wladimiroff have already addressed and explained very well how all three of us understand our role as amici curiae. Our position is, in fact, that if the need should arise, we might even separate our opinions and somebody may adopt a separate opinion. What I would like to ask is just for a few minutes of attention, as I come from a country of which the president, for a time, was Slobodan Milosevic. And I have to submit here a few important points linked to my position as a member of the amici curiae in such a case. I am not saying that in my own country I am in jeopardy in any physical sense, but from the moment I took over this duty as a member of the amici curiae, there were all kinds of criticisms as to why I had agreed to do this. Among other things, this was discussed in the Serbian parliament. Of course I will not discuss that. There was also some discussion at the Faculty of Law by all the law professors who had many objections as to why I had decided to accept this highly responsible job, the objection being that I am taking upon myself a enormous, an enormous moral, professional, and historical role. I don't like big words, highfalutin words. And this "historic" was used by others, not by me. I was also criticised for accepting to be an amicus curiae in this case, whereas those same law professors in Belgrade have offered their services to this Tribunal to act as amici curiae. I was particularly criticised from the moral standpoint, that I had dishonoured the Serb morality because, as you may know or not, from the middle of 1996 to the middle of 1997, I worked in a case, and I considered that to have been a great honour. I was Defence counsel in the Celebici case for Mr. Mucic. That case is in its final stages, and I submitted the opening arguments. But the main criticism then was as a Serb, I was defending a Croat in a case linked to a Muslim camp where the victims were Serbs alone. I said then and I have to repeat that now, that all of us, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, should be pleased to have had such a person, because he helped people not to have suffered more, and this should have been appreciated by both Serbs, Muslims and Croats, that there was such a person around. And at the time, I made a comparison with Schindler, saying that he was a Schindler among the Croats. However, here I am again in a position to be a part of this case, when both I and the accused come from the same state and belong to the same nation. Again the same criticisms and the same reproaches and risks for myself. I am profoundly convinced that I can perform the duty of amicus curiae as required by my duties as a professional lawyer according to the rules that apply throughout the world, and I am ready to bear full moral, professional, and even, if you will, historical responsibility to participate in these proceedings as an amicus curiae. Believe me, I have had to make that statement because of the situation I am in, and I hope you will not take it against me. To complement what has already been said before coming to my particular point, I think the principle of fairness is a universal principle, and we have a court which in time, space, and personnel has limited its jurisdiction to a small area on the globe. I'm quite confident that this Chamber can absolutely be fair, within the framework of the Rules, but that level of fairness would be absolute if the validity of those rules were to be universal. Until that is so -- and you know the problems there are in the establishment of a permanent international court, and until this Statute becomes universal, we will not be able to speak about absolute justice or fairness, which does not mean to say that I am not confident that this Chamber may be able to achieve absolute fairness, which perhaps will one day be achieved worldwide. To come now to the problem raised by Slobodan Milosevic in his correspondence and submissions, and that is he underlined in particular that his surrender to this Tribunal was not legal, was unlawful. And that brings me to the following issue: We cannot deny that at that point in time, he had been lawfully in detention according to the laws of Yugoslavia at the time. On the 28th of June, he was surrendered to this Tribunal and arrested according to the laws of the country earlier on. We also do not deny that he could have been surrendered by instruction of the Judge of this Tribunal, because detention had been ruled. However, who did the Tribunal or, rather, the Prosecution address via the Tribunal because the Tribunal issued an arrest warrant for the accused? Those requests mainly, or rather, entirely - they couldn't have gone otherwise - through the federal bodies, on the 24th of May, 1999, and on the 22nd of June, 2001, when Yugoslavia was again admitted to the United Nations. And this request was addressed to the federal organs, that is, the Federal Ministry of Justice, and giving primacy to the Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure, was entirely in the hands of the federal bodies of Yugoslavia. There is no dispute over that. There was communication between the two, and the federal minister responded. And what is most important of all, very soon the Federal Ministry of Justice undertook to draft a law which was later transferred into a decree on cooperation with the Hague Tribunal. There is no law in Yugoslavia on the extradition of a national to any foreign body. We have a law of extradition of foreign nationals. In view of that, the federal authorities undertook to pass a regulation in the form of a decree or a law that would enable cooperation with the Hague Tribunal. Therefore, what the Prosecution is alleging is not true, and that is that the primacy of the Tribunal is such that domestic legislation is totally unimportant. It cannot be unimportant. The fact that that state, as a member of the United Nations, undertook to pass regulations which would enable cooperation with the Hague Tribunal precisely as stipulated by the Rules and Statute of this Tribunal. And what happened then? Without waiting for that law to be passed, or rather, on the very day when the decree on establishing cooperation with the Hague Tribunal was in the final stages, whether it was before the Federal Constitutional Court, on that same day, the Republican Government decided to extradite Slobodan Milosevic to the Hague Tribunal, and as doing so, it acted arbitrarily. You know very well the provisions of international conventions. No one may arbitrarily jeopardise anyone, that everything has to be done in accordance with a certain procedure and according to a law. And Yugoslavia was investing special efforts to overcome the problem. You're aware of the Tadic case. Tadic was arrested in Germany. Germany worked for four months on the adoption of a law on the basis of which Tadic was extradited. So there was no reason not to wait, and this is something that the current President of Yugoslavia insisted upon in particular, that legitimacy be given to everything. There was no need to turn somebody into an ordinary object to be extradited. This was a decision taken by the government of the republic, which was not a member of the United Nations. It was only a member of the Federation, the Republic of Serbia, and it had no obligation to implement anything linked to international covenants to which Yugoslavia is a signatory. This is something that only the federal government had the right to decide about, federal organs through appropriate procedures, because they were doing everything to have the law adopted as soon as possible, and on the basis of that decree, to do what was necessary to establish cooperation with this Tribunal and thus enable everything else after that. By doing so, the state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was prevented from examining the instructions of the Judge of this Tribunal, and this is something that it should have been allowed to do, to examine the jurisdiction of this Tribunal and take the appropriate decision and act accordingly. Because everywhere in the world, including in this case, this procedure should have been respected, the right of the accused whose extradition was requested should have been respected. Only from Republika Srpska and now from Yugoslavia, people were extradited like objects, I have to say that. All I'm saying is that laws have to be respected. Now I come to my most important point. Slobodan Milosevic would not have been delivered in this way, because I assume if everything had been carried out according to procedure, the decree adopted, cooperation established, had there not been very great international pressure - and I'm sure that the Prosecution took part in this, and the Serbian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. government, when the law on cooperation with the Hague Tribunal was adopted, the Serbian government arbitrarily made the decision it made - as a result of such pressure on the national legislation, we now have Slobodan Milosevic here in this courtroom, and on the basis of such circumstances, it is not possible to base this case, and I mean the Prosecution. I must also say that I truly believe that you will devote special attention to this, and I think this is perhaps the most pressing problem to be addressed at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Now for the Prosecution. Who is going to address us? Madam Prosecutor, we've seen your brief which covers the matter, if I may say, very fully so we would be grateful if you could be fairly brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will be speaking in French which the accused does not speak, but I will speak slowly so that he can follow the English on the screen if he decides not to make use of the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's got an interpretation which is being played to him in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] I have to say that I had spoken in English in order to accommodate the accused during the other hearings, especially further to his refusal to put on a headset. But now, Mr. President and Your Honours, for me it is essential to be able to communicate with this Court in the other language of the Tribunal which comes more naturally to me and which allows me to express myself better in respect of the details, without any ambiguities creeping in. Mr. President and Your Honours, the accused Milosevic has said to us and has written to us and has repeated at the hearings, and I quote, "We are a nonexistent institution." This morning, the amici curiae have illustrated and have gone into depth in respect of all the themes of this preliminary motion, and I would like to say that since having heard them this morning, I must say that they acted the way assigned counsel would react. But, Mr. President, I'm not going to ask that counsel be assigned - things are as they are and I'm not going to insist - but I would simply like to take this opportunity to tell you that we have tried to get into contact with the amici curiae before this hearing. They refused to do so; they did not wish to meet with us, which I lament, in fact. This is to let you know what the problems are that we confront, these procedural difficulties, difficulties in respect to being able to prepare the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with that. I don't know anything about this. It's a matter for the amici the way that they choose to conduct this case, it is not a matter for the Court. If they choose to meet with the Prosecution, then that's a matter for them; but if they choose not to, equally it's a matter of them, and certainly there will be no criticism of them because of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was not a criticism, it was simply a factual observation. I would also ask that you allow me to say that I have had a study carried out on the right to self-representation. I have a study here, and I should say that the problem is opened for me, and it is true that customary international law does not contain the right to defend oneself without counsel. But I go back to the main point. The charges as -- the exchange of briefs and responses in writing in respect of the preliminary motion on jurisdiction, with all the things that follow upon that, is sufficiently well known. But even if sometimes one should not always repeat things, I would still like to repeat several of the most important points, the principal points in respect, first of all, of the legitimacy of this nonexistent institution. We have already three appeals judgements: the Tadic appeals judgement which, in fact, is an important judgement which deals with the substance of all the arguments raised here; we have the Aleksovski judgement which goes back and follows up on the Tadic judgement. And I believe that the three principles which have been recalled by the Appeals Chamber are untouchable here. By this I mean the establishment of a hierarchy of the administration of justice by ruling on questions of fact and law, the guarantee of the need for security and the foreseeability, and the rule of international customary law, that is, the right to appeal, which means, therefore, the accused's right to have all of these matters dealt with in the same way. For this reason, the Trial Chamber complies with the judgements of the Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber itself is following its own decisions, and we heard this morning through the amici curiae that the exchange of these cases -- of these matters has been decided. The judgement in Celebici really simply confirms what has already been set forth as a principle. And I would like to say to you, Your Honours, that we have no interest and no demands in respect of asking for outside opinions. This advisory opinion which has been the subject of great pressure is not necessary insofar as these decisions were already taken in previous cases. We are requesting, Mr. President, that the accused Milosevic recognise our jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. The international community has created this Tribunal with limited territorial jurisdiction, that's true, but we do not have temporal restriction as was said this morning. We are asking, Mr. President, Your Honours, we are asking for the power to begin a trial against Mr. Milosevic. The three other principal reasons that I'm going to mention here are the Prosecutor's independence, because that is what is at stake here. In respect of the independence of the Court, there can be no challenge, because that's in law; and in respect that the Security Council urged the Prosecutor to do what she is doing must be an element which falls within the category of lack of independence. I point out to the Tribunal Resolution 1160 of 31 March 1998, whereas the Prosecutor announced on the 10th of March, 1998, in public, that the investigation into what happened in Kosovo was going to begin. Therefore, I believe that that small press release of the 10th of March, 1998 should be given the importance that it deserves. Likewise, if the Security Council requested or urged the Prosecutor, what does that really mean? It simply means that the Prosecutor should be reminded of her original mandate in respect of the resolution which established this Tribunal; and in the second place, being involved in opening an investigation does not mean that one is going to immediately issue an indictment. In respect of the Prosecutor's discretionary powers, Mr. President, I cannot agree that this be put into question, and I have no justification to provide for saying that. I heard this morning what was said. I don't have to provide any proof. This is a discretionary power subject to the mandate from the Security Council, and that is it. We are asking to be able to bring a trial against Mr. Milosevic, a former head of state, and this is the second argument, former head of state. Here people do not want to understand. People don't want to understand that this Tribunal was established by the international community explicitly in order to put an end to the impunity of the powerful people, the heads of states, and, therefore, a review of their individual criminal responsibility in the exercise of their function is the task of this Tribunal. Permit me to say, Mr. President, that outside the Tribunal there are thousands of victims who are demanding justice. For this reason, no immunity for anybody, when what is involved are war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. The Secretary-General's report to the Security Council in respect of the establishment of this Tribunal leaves absolutely no doubt on that issue, because we know that the heads of state entail more significant responsibility for serious violations of international humanitarian law. Today, Mr. President, this is the turn of the accused Milosevic, who is complaining - my last point - about an illegal transfer. I followed very carefully the transfer of the accused Milosevic, and I must tell you that he was arrested pursuant to a national warrant of arrest in his own country, and was transferred further to a decision of the government of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Yugoslavia, on the basis of a decree which was accepted and then suspended. I am not going to go through the legislative CV of what happened in Yugoslavia, but this has absolutely nothing to do with the international obligation that we are familiar with, Article 29 of the Statute. The only thing I say is that at the time Yugoslavia became a member state of the United Nations, that obligation for Yugoslavia existed further to the obligations that every state would have. So the decision to transfer the accused was taken with full respect for the international obligations. One final point, Mr. President - you'll see that I was very brief - is the fact that the amici curiae, the counsel, are asking to allow him to speak. I must say that we have some problems in respect of the review of the exculpatory documents because we do not have a person to speak with. I believe that I should find -- I must find a solution, and I call upon precedents in order to find that solution. Is it the accused himself that's going to look through all the documents? I'm now speaking about the application of Rule 68 which is just as important to me as any other application of the procedural Rules. All this is to say to you, Mr. President, that I feel we must allow him to speak, that is, the accused Milosevic, of course within the limits that we set forth. I thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, if I understand the argument of the amici on the question of transfer, it is that the obligation under Article 29 of the Statute is an obligation of the state. In this respect, they are saying that the arrest warrants were issued to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when, in fact, the arrest and transfer were effected by the government of Serbia. In that circumstance, they would see, as I understand it, that Rule 58 would not apply. Rule 58, as you know, is a Rule which says that the obligations in Article 29 prevail over any legal impediment to the surrender of an accused to the Tribunal. Now, their contention is that the obligation is the obligation of the Federal Republic. What was implemented was a transfer by the Government of Serbia, and they contend that for that reason, the transfer is illegal. I raise this because you refer to Article 29, but what they're saying is that Article 29 was not complied with and that Rule 58 would be inapplicable. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As you know, in the Yugoslav Federation, the central government of the Federation has no executing power; that is, all transfers, all decisions by the police or any bindings measures taken are carried out by the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia which executes and caries out the arrests and transfers, which is the case of the other accused who came from Belgrade. It is true that the decision is the one taken by the Federation. Now, the decision itself -- itself of the transfer is the Federation and Prime Minister Djindjic clearly mentioned the fact that the decision to carry out the transfer was taken and accepted by the Federation, but the very execution not only of the accused Milosevic of all things done by the police and the arrests that is were carried out and transfers that were made and searches, all of those fall within the province of the Republic of Serbia, and that is why the transport itself was carried out by the republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are saying that this was properly the responsibility of the Government of Serbia, the transfer?

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. It is the Republic of Serbia which must execute the transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, I believe you would also say that the matter of the internal constitutional organisation of a state is irrelevant in a situation like this. There is a rule, Article 27 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties which prevents a party from invoking the provisions of its internal law as a justification for its failure to perform a treaty obligation. There is a treaty obligation here, and it must be performed. In your brief, you -- I believe you mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is mentioned, that is, Rule 58 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it says that the obligations --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "any legal impediment to the surrender of transfer of the accused to the Tribunal which must exist under the national law or extradition treaties of the state concerned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The new point for me is what you say, that it was in fact the responsibility of the Government of Serbia to affect this transfer. Perhaps we'll hear a response from that from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, there is really two points that I want to cover before the adjournment. The first is this: You refer to customary international law not containing a right to defend oneself. I find that most surprising if it really does say that. It seems a fundamental right for anybody in a court to defend yourself. Maybe we can go into that at some other time. The other point is the point about exculpatory evidence which of course is an important one, and it would seem to be sensible to discuss that during the Status Conference and decide what way of proceeding in relation to obligations in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. As regards defending oneself, I can give you the study that I had carried out by my specialist. It's a few pages long. It's interesting to read. And as regards the rest, Mr. President, we have to discuss that at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appropriate time, because indeed it is important. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can pass that document through. There is no reason to say that we will be bound by it. We will adjourn now until half past, when we'll hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now your opportunity to address us on the motions before us today. There's no need to repeat what's in the written submissions because we've read all those. It's also your opportunity to address us on the Prosecution motion to amend the indictment, if there's anything you want to say about that, it's now your chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first place, I am not submitting any motions to this Court because I do not recognise this Court. If what I am saying into this microphone is considered by you to be a submission on my part, that's up to you. Secondly, with respect to amicus curiae, it is my understanding that your explanation, when appointing the amicus curiae, was that thereby a contribution would be made to a fair trial, if in such an illegal proceedings one can talk of a fair trial. I think in doing so, you have added a new concept to a set of new concepts, because now we are in a situation when two teams are working for the cause of the same party. So this could now be termed as the "Hague fair play." As for this flood of new amendments and indictments, this deluge cannot flood and cover up the truth, because the truth is known to millions of people. I have heard here, as I heard on the previous occasion, some concern because I am not reading the documents from this false indictment, because allegedly I should know what I am charged with. Let me tell you, I know very well what I am being accused of. I have been accused because in a legal way and with legitimate means on the basis of the right to self-determination that belongs to every nation, I defended my nation. I had the honour to defend my nation from the criminal aggression carried out against it, and to defend my people from terrorism whereby the Clinton Administration cooperated closely with. And this is also something that no one will be able to deny. The truth cannot be sunk by any kind of flood of false accusations. And I have no intention still to familiarise myself with the contents of something that has been totally fabricated and that is far from the truth. As for the polemics I have been listening to as to who was competent and who was not and whether a particular government should have done something prior to another government, I wonder and am astonished that not even the attorney from Belgrade, a member of the amicus curiae, that he should be speaking about competencies while forgetting that no government had the competence to enter into arrangements whereby the Constitution of Serbia and the Constitution of Yugoslavia was being violated. I'm glad that the gentlemen from the amicus curiae are aware that they cannot speak on my behalf and that I have nothing in common with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider the motions, preliminary motions, on which we've been addressed this morning. We've had the opportunity of considering the application to amend the indictment, and I'll give our ruling on that. Rule 50 does not spell out any test to be applied in deciding whether leave to amend an indictment should be given. However, the cases in the Tribunal show that the fundamental question is whether the amendment would cause injustice or prejudice to the accused if it were granted. In determining whether prejudice or injustice does arise, the issues a Trial Chamber must have in mind include the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial, including adequate time for preparation. On the other hand, the Prosecution are entitled to amend an indictment provided that the amendment is necessary and can be done without prejudicing the accused's right to a fair and expeditious trial. A Trial Chamber must balance these factors in coming to a decision. In the present case, the amendments substantially amount to the addition of one count, the particularising of another count, the particularising of a theory of responsibility together with a modest increase in the factual allegations, to add a number of deportation sites to those already in the indictment, and to add some other factual matters. We have in mind that this is the second amendment to an indictment which is already two years old, but any trial on this indictment is more than three months away at least, and the accused, therefore, has adequate time for preparation. These amendments amount to a relatively insubstantial change in the indictment and occasion no prejudice or unfairness to the accused. In fact, they amount to an improvement by clarifying the Prosecution case, in particular, on joint enterprise and persecution. Accordingly, leave to amend the indictment will be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We now turn to the next stage, which is the reading of the Kosovo indictment. The second amended indictment will now be read, as Rule 62 provides, in a language which the accused speaks and understands. Let the indictment be read.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor of the International Tribunal against Slobodan Milosevic and others. Second Amended Indictment. The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, charges Slobodan Milosevic and others with crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war as set forth below. Accused. Slobodan Milosevic was born on the 20th of August, 1941, in the town of Pozarevac in present-day Republic of Serbia. In 1964, he received a law degree from the University of Belgrade and began a career in management and banking. Slobodan Milosevic held the posts of deputy director and later general director at Tehnogas, a major gas company until 1978. Thereafter, he became president of Beogradska banka, one of the largest banks in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY, and held that post until 1983. In 1983, Slobodan Milosevic began his political career. He became Chairman of the City Committee of the League of Communists of Belgrade in 1984. In 1986, he was elected Chairman of the Presidium of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia, and was re-elected in 1988. On the 16th of July, 1990, the League of Communists of Serbia and the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of Serbia were united. A new party was named the Socialist Party of Serbia, or the SPS, and Slobodan Milosevic was elected its president. He continued to hold the post of the President of the SPS as of the date of this indictment. Slobodan Milosevic was elected President of the Presidency of Serbia on the 8th of May, 1989, and re-elected on the 5th of December that same year. After the adoption of the new constitution of Serbia on the 28th of September, 1990, Slobodan Milosevic was elected to the newly established office of President of Serbia in multiparty elections held on the 9th and 26th of December, 1990. He was re-elected on the 20th of December, 1992. After serving two terms as President of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic was elected President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or the FRY, on the 15th of July, 1997, and he began his official duties on the 23rd of July, 1997. Following defeat in the September 2000 FRY presidential elections, Slobodan Milosevic stepped down from this position on the 6th of October, 2000. At all times relevant to this indictment, Slobodan Milosevic held the post of President of the FRY. Paragraphs 5 to 15 deal with other individuals; therefore, we continue with the reading of the indictment as of paragraph 16. Individual Criminal Responsibility. Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Each of the accused is individually responsible for the crimes alleged against him in this indictment under Articles 3, 5, and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The accused planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of these crimes. By using the word "committed" in this indictment, the Prosecutor does not intend to suggest that any of the accused physically perpetrated any of the crimes charged personally. "Committing" in this indictment refers to participation in a joint criminal enterprise as a co-perpetrator. The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was inter alia the expulsion of a substantial portion of the Kosovo Albanian population from the territory of the province of Kosovo in an effort to ensure continued Serbian control over the province. To fulfil this criminal purpose, each of the accused, acting individually or in concert with each other, and with others known and unknown, significantly contributed to the joint criminal enterprise using the de jure and de facto powers available to him. This joint criminal enterprise came into existence no later than October 1998, and continued throughout the time period when the crimes alleged in Counts 1 to 5 of this indictment occurred, beginning on or about the 1st of January, 1999 and continuing until the 20th of June, 1999. A number of individuals participated in this joint criminal enterprise during the entire duration of its existence, or alternatively at different times during the duration of its existence, including the accused Slobodan Milosevic and others known and unknown. The crimes enumerated in Counts 1 to 5 in this indictment were within the object of the joint criminal enterprise. Alternatively, the crimes enumerated in Counts 3 to 5 were natural and foreseeable consequences of the joint criminal enterprise, and the accused were aware that such crimes were the likely outcome of the joint criminal enterprise. Despite their awareness of the foreseeable consequences, Slobodan Milosevic and others known and unknown knowingly and wilfully participated in the joint criminal enterprise. Each of the accused and other participants in the joint criminal enterprise shared the intent and state of mind required for the commission of each of the crimes charged in Counts 1 to 5. On this basis, under Article 7(1) of the Statute, each of the accused and other participants in the joint criminal enterprise bear individual criminal responsibility for the crimes alleged in Counts 1 to 5. Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Slobodan Milosevic and other accused, while holding positions of superior authority, are also individually criminally responsible for the acts or omissions of their subordinates pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Slobodan Milosevic was elected President of the FRY on the 15th of July, 1997, and assumed office on the 23rd of July, 1997. At all times relevant to this indictment he held the post of President of the FRY. As President of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic was President of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY. The Supreme Defence Council consists of the President of the FRY and the Presidents of the member republics Serbia and Montenegro. The Supreme Defence Council decides on the National Defence Plan and issues decisions concerning the VJ or Yugoslav army. As President of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic had the power to order implementation of the National Defence Plan and command the VJ in war and peace, pursuant to decisions made by the Supreme Defence Council. Slobodan Milosevic, as Supreme Commander of the VJ, performed these duties through commands, orders, and decisions. Under the FRY Law on Defence, as Supreme Commander of the VJ, Slobodan Milosevic also exercised command authority over republican police units subordinated to the VJ during a state of imminent threat of war or a state of war. A declaration of imminent threat of war was proclaimed on the 23rd of March, 1999, and a state of war, on the 24th of March, 1999. In addition to his de jure powers, at all times relevant to this indictment, Slobodan Milosevic exercised extensive de facto control over numerous institutions essential to or involved in the conduct of the offences alleged herein. Slobodan Milosevic exercised extensive de facto control over federal institutions nominally under the competence of the assembly or the government of the FRY. Slobodan Milosevic also exercised de facto control over functions and institutions nominally under the competence of Serbia and its autonomous provinces including the Serbian police force. Slobodan Milosevic further exercised de facto control over numerous aspects of the FRY's political and economic life, particularly the media. Between 1986 and the early 1990s, Slobodan Milosevic progressively required de facto control over these federal, republican, provincial, and other institutions. Slobodan Milosevic's de facto control over Serbian, SFRY, FRY, and other state organs stemmed in part from his leadership of the two principal political parties that ruled in Serbia from 1986 to 2000, and in the FRY from 1992 to the year 2000. From 1986 until 1990, he was Chairman of the Presidium of the Central Committee of the League of Communists in Serbia, then the ruling party in Serbia. In 1990, he was elected President of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the successor party to the League of Communists of Serbia and the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of Serbia. Throughout the period of his Presidency of Serbia from 1990 to 1997 and as the President of the FRY from 1997 to the year 2000 Slobodan Milosevic was also the leader of the SPS. Following the commencement of the joint criminal enterprise beginning on or about the 1st of January, 1999, and continuing until 20th of June, 1999, Slobodan Milosevic and others known and unknown planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at Kosovo Albanian civilians living in Kosovo in the FRY. The deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at the Kosovo Albanian population was executed by the forces of the FRY and Serbia acting at the direction, with the encouragement, or with the support of Slobodan Milosevic and others known and unknown. Forces of the FRY and Serbia undertook the operations targeting the Kosovo Albanians with the objective of expelling a substantial portion of the Kosovo Albanian population from Kosovo in an effort to ensure continued Serbian control over the province. To achieve this objective, the forces of the FRY and Serbia, acting in concert, engaged in well-planned and coordinated operations as described in paragraphs 55 to 61. The forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner forcibly expelled hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes and internally displaced them within Kosovo. To facilitate these expulsions and displacements, forces of the FRY and Serbia intentionally created an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force, and acts of violence. Throughout Kosovo, the forces of FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian citizens. This was accomplished by the widespread shelling of towns and villages, the burning and destruction of property, including homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments, and religious sites, and the destruction of personal property. As a result of these orchestrated actions, villages, towns, and entire regions were made uninhabitable for Kosovo Albanians. In addition to the deliberate destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians, forces of the FRY and Serbia committed widespread or systematic acts of brutality and violence against Kosovo Albanian civilians in order to perpetuate the climate of fear, create chaos and a pervading fear for life. Forces of the FRY and Serbia went from village to village and in the towns and cities, from area to area, threatening and expelling the Kosovo Albanian population. Kosovo Albanians were frequently intimidated, assaulted, or killed in public view to enforce the departure of their families and neighbours. Many Kosovo Albanians, who were not directly forcibly expelled from their communities, fled as a result of the climate of terror created by the widespread or systematic beatings, harassment, sexual assaults, unlawful arrests, killings, shelling, and looting carried out across the province. Forces of the FRY and Serbia persistently subjected Kosovo Albanians to insults, racial slurs, degrading acts and other forms of physical and psychological mistreatment based on their racial, religious, and political identification. All sectors of Kosovo Albanian society were displaced including women, children, the elderly, and the infirm. Thousands of Kosovo Albanians who fled their homes as a result of the conduct of the forces of the FRY and Serbia and the deliberate climate of terror that pervaded the territory the Kosovo, joined convoys of persons that moved towards Kosovo's borders with the Republic of Albania and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Across the routes from the border crossings forces of the FRY and Serbia manned checkpoints where the displaced Kosovo Albanians were subjected to further beatings, extortion, robbery, harassment, assaults, illegal arrests, and killings. At other times, forces of the FRY and Serbia escorted groups of expelled Kosovo Albanians to the borders. By these methods, the forces of the FRY and Serbia maintained control over the movement of displaced Kosovo Albanians to the borders. Displaced Kosovo Albanians often arrived at the borders of Kosovo on foot in convoys of several thousand persons, or carried by tractors, trailers, and trucks, as well as on trains, buses, or trucks which were organised and provided by forces of the FRY and Serbia. In addition, thousands of Kosovo Albanians who fled their homes and were thereby forcibly transferred as a result of the conduct of the forces of the FRY and Serbia and the deliberate climate of terror that persuaded the territory of Kosovo were forced to seek shelter for days, weeks, or months in other towns and villages and/or in forests and mountains throughout the province. Some of these internally displaced persons remained inside the province of Kosovo throughout the time period relevant to this indictment, and many persons died as a consequence of the harsh weather conditions, insufficient food, inadequate medical attention, and exhaustion. Others eventually crossed over one of the Kosovo borders into Albania, Macedonia, Montenegro, or crossed the provincial boundary between Kosovo and Serbia. Forces of the FRY and Serbia controlled and coordinated the movements of many internally displaced Kosovo Albanians until they were finally expelled from Kosovo. . Throughout Kosovo, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic effort to deter expelled Kosovo Albanians from returning to their homes, forces of the FRY and Serbia looted and pillaged the personal and commercial property belonging to Kosovo Albanians. Forces of the FRY and Serbia used wholesale searches, threats of force and acts of violence to rob Kosovo Albanians of money and valuables. And in a widespread or systematic manner, authorities at FRY border posts stole personal vehicles and other property from Kosovo Albanians being deported from the province. In addition, throughout Kosovo, forces of the FRY and Serbia systematically seized and destroyed the personal identity documents and licenses of vehicles belonging to Kosovo Albanian civilians. As Kosovo Albanians were forced from their homes and directed towards Kosovo's borders, they were subjected to demands to surrender identity documents at selected points en route to border crossings and at border crossings with Albanian and Macedonia. These actions were undertaken in order to erase any record of the deported Kosovo Albanians presence in Kosovo and to deny them the right to return to their homes. Count 1. Deportation.
